title: Persistent Systems Skips Campus Hiring in FY27, Pivots to Lateral Recruitment
excerpt: The Pune-based IT services firm will focus on experienced hires aligned to project demand, even as it posts record quarterly revenue and pursues a €1.27 billion acquisition of Germany's Nagarro.
body:
• Persistent Systems will not conduct campus hiring in FY27, shifting entirely to lateral recruitment matched to project demand, CEO Sandeep Kalra confirmed
  • The company posted Q1 FY27 revenue of $452.4 million — its 25th consecutive quarter of growth — with a record total contract value of $1.15 billion
  • The €1.27 billion acquisition of German IT firm Nagarro, announced in June, aims to expand Persistent's European footprint from 9% to roughly 30% of revenue

No Freshers This Year

Persistent Systems, one of India's fastest-growing mid-tier IT services companies, has decided to skip campus hiring entirely for FY27, pivoting instead to lateral recruitment aligned to specific project demand. CEO Sandeep Kalra confirmed the shift during the company's Q1 FY27 earnings discussion, citing the need to match talent acquisition to the increasingly specialized nature of client requirements.

https://x.com/moneycontrolcom/status/2084821440650727680

The decision reflects a broader recalibration across India's IT sector, where demand for fresh engineering graduates has cooled even as the appetite for experienced professionals with AI, cloud, and data engineering skills continues to rise. Persistent's move is notable because the Pune-based firm has historically maintained an active campus program spanning over 250 university partnerships.

Record Quarter, Record Deals

The hiring pivot comes against a backdrop of strong financial performance. Persistent reported Q1 FY27 revenue of $452.4 million, up 3.8% sequentially and 16.1% year-over-year, marking its 25th consecutive quarter of revenue growth — one of the longest such streaks in the Indian IT sector.

The headline number, however, was eclipsed by a record total contract value of $1.15 billion for the quarter. A single strategic services agreement with a leading global technology company, worth over $650 million across 6.5 years, contributed to the milestone.

EBIT margin came in at 16.0%, reflecting 32.7% year-over-year growth, a significant improvement that underscores the company's operational discipline even as it invests heavily in acquisitions and AI capabilities.

The Nagarro Bet

Persistent's biggest strategic move of the year is the €1.27 billion acquisition of Nagarro, a German IT services firm with deep roots in European markets. The deal, announced in June, is designed to address a structural gap: Europe currently accounts for just 9% of Persistent's revenue, compared with over 80% from North America.

"Building that presence organically would have taken years and required substantial investment. This is a God-given opportunity."

— Sandeep Kalra, CEO, Persistent Systems

Kalra rejected suggestions that the acquisition was a play to buy growth because Persistent's core business was slowing. "We don't work for the stock movements. We work to build a company that is built to last," he told CNBC-TV18. The transaction values Nagarro at approximately 1.2 times revenue and nine times EBITDA, according to CFO Vinit Teredesai.

The acquisition drew initial investor scepticism — Persistent's shares fell more than 11% following the announcement — but management has committed to making the deal EPS-accretive from year one, with a combined EBITDA margin target of 17-18%.

An Industry-Wide Shift

Persistent's decision to skip campus hiring mirrors a pattern across India's IT sector. After years of mass fresher intake — TCS alone targeted 40,000 campus hires in peak years — the industry has shifted toward demand-driven, project-specific recruitment. Campus hiring across major IT firms has remained limited, while walk-in drives increasingly focus on experienced professionals in AI, machine learning, and data engineering.

The implications extend beyond corporate strategy. India's engineering colleges produce roughly 1.5 million graduates annually, many of whom depend on IT sector campus drives as their primary pathway to employment. A sustained pullback in fresher hiring could widen the gap between the skills India's education system produces and what its highest-growth employers actually need.

What's Ahead

For Persistent, the priorities are clear: integrate Nagarro, maintain its growth streak, and continue scaling AI-driven service lines. The company has set a revenue aspiration of $5 billion by FY31, a target that depends on successful European expansion and sustained large-deal momentum.

Whether campus hiring returns in FY28 will depend on how quickly the Nagarro integration proceeds and whether client demand shifts in ways that favour generalist talent over specialists. For now, the message from Pune is unambiguous: experienced hires only.
